title: Rowan and the Little Dragon's Giggle
markdown:
The Lantern Valleys of Starfall Range glowed softly, a sleepy light that never got too bright. In a cozy cottage tucked between bushes full of glow-worms lived Rowan, a young wizard with bright curious eyes and always a smudge of ink on one finger. His constant friend was Anwen, a goat not known for being brave. She did not climb tall wobbly rocks. She was famous for finding the best, coziest places to take naps. Other goats munched juicy clover. Anwen munched on dreams. Her fluffy beard twitched as she slept. She could nap anywhere: standing up, walking, or even mid-chew on a dandelion.

One cool morning the air smelled like lavender. Rowan was trying a tricky spell. He wanted his inkwell to shine like a captured star. So far it just made a faint blue shimmer and a great many ink smudges on his nose and chin. As he concentrated, trying to get a spark from his wand, he heard two tiny pixies buzzing like bees near pretty blue flowers.

“The Whispering Woods,” one pixie chirped, wings fluttering like a nervous butterfly. “They say the trees sing old secrets to anyone who listens with their heart. And the mushrooms… oh, the mushrooms. They giggle when sunbeams tickle them.”

Rowan’s eyes grew wide. Trees that sang? Mushrooms that giggled? The most wonderfully silly story he had ever heard. He guessed it was probably made-up. He loved stories that might be a little bit true. He loved the edge of what was real.

“Anwen,” he called, too loud for a goat enjoying a big nap under a cheerful daisy. Anwen had been dreaming of a field of soft moss and warm sunshine. She blinked open one sleepy eye, brown like rich chocolate. “Let’s go exploring. To the Whispering Woods.”

Anwen made a long slow maaaa that sounded more like a sigh than a bleat. Rowan, always happy, took it for agreement. “Great,” he said, grabbing his bag. Anwen secretly hoped the woods had a nice sunny patch of moss for a nap.

The path into the Whispering Woods was a ribbon of light. Sunlight peeked through leaves the colour of old favourite books. Rowan’s heart thumped. He could not wait to hear the trees hum their secrets. Anwen seemed more interested in the ground. She sniffed at roots and peeked into shady spots. Suddenly she stopped, perfectly still, fluffy ears perked. Rowan followed her gaze.

Leaning against a big old oak was a wheelbarrow that looked a bit sad. One wheel wobbled. It had a patch of rust like a ginger beard. Rowan did not think much of it. Anwen snorted, then nudged the wheelbarrow with her wet black nose. It creaked softly. She snorted again, this time sounding very annoyed, as if the wheelbarrow were too loud and clumsy. A funny quiet argument started. Anwen stared hard. The wheelbarrow creaked in the breeze. She answered with a deep maaaa that clearly meant she was watching that noisy thing.

Rowan tried to ignore the goat-and-wheelbarrow drama and walked a little deeper. The air became very quiet and calm. Then a tiny puff of smoke, sweet, like sugar just starting to toast. Curious, he tiptoed around a mossy log that felt soft as velvet. There, sitting on a fallen acorn, was a creature no bigger than his teacup.

A dragon. Not a fire-breathing sort. Scales like shiny green jewels. Wings thin and colourful, beating fast, keeping it hovering above the acorn. It coughed, a small soft sound. A tiny puff of smoke smelling like toasted marshmallows floated into the air.

“Hello,” Rowan whispered. He did not want to scare it.

The tiny dragon blinked big amber eyes. “H-hello,” it squeaked, voice like little bells. “I’m Puffkin.”

Rowan’s smile grew. “I’m Rowan. And this is Anwen,” he said, pointing back. Anwen was still giving the wheelbarrow a stern look. “She’s having a little disagreement with that wheelbarrow.”

Puffkin tilted its tiny head. Green scales caught the light. Then it let out a little happy giggle. It was not a mushroom, but it was definitely giggling. The sound was as sweet as honey. Rowan felt a wave of pure wonder. He watched Puffkin chase a sunbeam, scales flashing like a disco ball for ladybugs. Anwen, forgetting the wheelbarrow, stopped scolding and watched the little dragon with wide curious eyes. The woods, even without singing trees or giggling mushrooms, held a quiet special hush.

There were no singing trees. There were no giggling mushrooms, not the way the pixies had said. Walking back toward the Lantern Valleys, with Puffkin perched happily on his shoulder still smelling a bit like toasted marshmallows, and Anwen trotting beside him, glancing suspiciously at the distant silent wheelbarrow, Rowan did not feel cheated. He had found a tiny wonderful friend. Anwen found something worth staying awake for, at least until the next sunny patch. Puffkin giggled again, and a mushroom by the path did not answer, which was quite all right. The giggle was already in the bag, riding home on a wizard’s shoulder.
